evidence_quotes.quote: The focus of this paper is to explore the roles local governments can and should play to enable private sector participation in WASH service delivery in South East Asia. We draw on research undertaken in Indonesia, Vietnam, and Cambodia to illustrate the various ways local governments have become engaged with small-scale WASH enterprises.

The findings demonstrate important local government roles, including: training and business development support to enterprises; linking demand and supply by promoting local enterprises; supporting associations of entrepreneurs; providing targeted subsidies or financing to catalyse private sector engagement or to facilitate access for the poor and disadvantaged; and setting and monitoring quality standards and accreditation of products and services.
Interviewees reported caps on water tariffs and complicated bureaucracy, which were both unconducive to private sector participation.

Qualitative analysis was conducted using primary data, coupled with analysis of WASH and private sector policy and other relevant literature to explore the ways in which local governments engage small-scale enterprises, and the challenges they face.

Across all countries, we did not find any evidence of cases where local governments alone had provided subsidies or financing through enterprises to ensure the poor and disadvantaged were reached; although, given the human right to sanitation, it could be argued that this is a critical role they should be playing.
Our research also revealed that ensuring equity in access is a key local government role, but very little evidence of local government activity in this area was observed.

criterion_notes.c1: Although situated in the rural WASH sector and framed around SDG 6 and the human right to water and sanitation, the study empirically examines local government support to and engagement with small-scale WASH enterprises and market systems rather than household or community water or sanitation service access.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording: YES — the paper examines institutional, administrative, policy, and regulatory roles of local governments and political-economy dynamics in the rural WASH sector. Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: NO — the empirical analysis focuses predominantly on generic business-development training and enterprise support, behavioural/demand promotion (CLTS, awareness visits, sales promotion), support for entrepreneur associations, and broad decentralized political-economy background shaping support to private market actors, rather than a rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community service access. Isolated brief mentions of water tariff caps and bureaucracy in Cambodia, a provincial law phasing out connection fees in Tien Giang, a commune rule requiring new house builders to commit to a latrine, CPC payment mediation, and an NGO voucher's administrative cost are cited only in relation to enterprise market participation or local government roles without analysing how rules govern household access.
criterion_notes.c3: Empirical qualitative multi-country political economy study conducted in Vietnam and Indonesia (2014-2016) and Cambodia (2016-2017) using primary semi-structured interviews across 86 organizations (130 interviewees in Table 1), a stakeholder workshop, and policy document analysis.
criterion_notes.c4: Fails Criterion 4: the paper reports qualitative findings on local government enterprise-support roles, stakeholder perceptions, and barriers to private-sector WASH market participation, but reports no empirical outcome measuring or assessing household or community water or sanitation access, connection, service availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion.
criterion_notes.c5: The study design, organizational sample/unit of analysis (government agencies, NGOs, donors, and small-scale WASH enterprises), political-economy exposure, and enterprise-support outcome are identifiable from the full text (noting minor discrepancies between prose and Table 1 counts on p. 5), though no eligible household/community service-access outcome is measured.

study_design: Qualitative multi-country political economy study using semi-structured interviews, stakeholder workshop, and policy/literature analysis
population_and_sample: National and subnational government agencies, small-scale private and social WASH enterprises, NGOs, and donors across Vietnam (44 organizations, 76 interviewees), Cambodia (21 organizations, 16 interviewees in Table 1; prose also notes a 14-participant workshop and 7 sanitation enterprise interviews), and Indonesia (21 organizations in Table 1 / 29 in prose, 38 interviewees); unit of analysis is the local government and WASH enterprise/sector relationship
exposure: Political economy dynamics, national and local policies, decentralization, coverage targets, and local government support and regulatory practices toward small-scale WASH enterprises
outcome: Local government roles, activities, and constraints in supporting small-scale WASH enterprises and enabling private-sector WASH market participation (no household or community service access, connection, availability, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion outcome reported)
rationale: Excluded under E04 (Wrong outcome), with additional failure on Criterion 1 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type scope of Criterion 2. Although this qualitative political-economy study in Vietnam, Cambodia, and Indonesia is empirical (c3=yes), its unit of analysis and reported findings concern how local governments support and engage small-scale WASH enterprises (business training, demand promotion, entrepreneur associations, quality certification, and conditions for private-sector market participation). It reports no empirical outcome on household or community water or sanitation access, connection, service availability, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion (c4=no), and under the 2026-10-13 clarification of Criterion 2 its focus is enterprise facilitation, behavioural demand promotion, and macro/sector political economy rather than rule-type mechanisms directly governing household service access (c2=no).
